Standard & Poor’s (S&P) today downgraded the rating of Mozambique’s domestic debt issues to CCC-, maintained the level of external debt issues, but worsened the outlook for both to negative.
“The government announced a plan to carry out liability management exercises on its local currency obligations. In general, we consider most debt swaps in the CCC category to be distressed and equivalent to a financial default,” write the analysts from the financial rating agency.
In the note announcing the downgrade of the rating for domestic debt issues, S&P points out that “post-election economic disruptions are negatively influencing the government’s budgetary and liquidity operations,” which contributed to the downgrade of the opinion on the quality of debt issues in meticais made in Mozambique.
In addition to downgrading the rating of domestic operations, S&P decided to maintain its opinion on the quality of sovereign credit in international debt issues, known as Eurobonds, but downgraded its assessment of the evolution of these ratings, signalling that a further downgrade in both cases is likely in the next 12 to 18 months.
In its analysis of the Mozambican economy, S&P foresees a widening of the budget deficit to 4.5% between 2025 and 2028, worsening the 4.2% forecast made in October last year, due to “falls in tax revenue, increased spending on security and weaker growth due to recent demonstrations”.
The Mozambican government is expected to meet private banks soon to discuss a debt swap with maturities in March, May and September, “which should involve an extension of terms and a review of interest rates”, and could lead to the attribution of a default “if the final terms of the exercise of debt liabilities resemble a distressed debt swap”, warns S&P.
The agency added that the analysis is made on a case-by-case basis and takes into account the political and macroeconomic context.
Mozambique is servicing its external debt without delay, which is worth 9% of GDP and costs US$81 million, around €77.5 million, per year until 2028, and increases to US$225 million (€215 million) per year between 2028 and 2031, before gas production in the north of the country begins, possibly in 2030, says S&P, warning, however, that “there remains a risk that the US$20 billion (€19.1 billion) Area 1 project could suffer further delays”.
Regarding external financing, which is essential for Mozambique to balance its public accounts, S&P analysts say that “the baseline scenario assumes that Mozambique will continue to access financing under the three-year program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), worth US$456 million (€436 million), but the budgetary slippage could postpone the last two disbursements, which cumulatively amount to US$126 million (€120 million), and jeopardize the potential signing of a new program after March 2025”.
In 2023, Mozambique also received US$664 million, around €636 million, in financing from the United States agency for international development, USAID, so “the current suspension of US financing worsens already difficult external financing conditions”. S&P also predicts that Mozambique will return to more significant growth, of 4.3%, above the 2.5% recorded last year due to the post-election protests in the last quarter, then growing, on average, 5.4% a year until 2028.

a4148.t:
Conflict, climate change, epidemics, and displacement are converging to create an unparalleled global health crisis, with 305 million people in urgent need of humanitarian assistance in 2025. In response, the World Health Organization (WHO) is calling for US$ 1.5 billion for its 2025 Health Emergency Appeal (HEA), to support life-saving health interventions worldwide.
The appeal, launched today by WHO Director-General, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, outlines the critical priorities and resources needed to address 42 ongoing health emergencies, including 17 Grade 3 crises – the most severe emergencies requiring the highest level of response. With health systems stretched to their limits and global financial resources dwindling, the US$ 1.5 billion are needed to help people facing the most difficult situations
“Conflicts, outbreaks, climate-related disasters and other health emergencies are no longer isolated or occasional – they are relentless, overlapping and intensifying,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. “From controlling cholera outbreaks to providing mental health support in conflict zones, WHO’s work extends beyond the immediate care we provide. We empower communities to protect themselves, prioritize equity, and build a legacy of preparedness. This appeal is about enabling WHO to save lives, protect the right to health, and provide hope where there is none.”
A coordinated response to protect vulnerable populations
WHO is committed to delivering emergency health assistance, including in conflict zones such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the occupied Palestinian territory and Sudan. WHO’s response in emergencies is aligned with wider humanitarian efforts and prioritizes providing essential care and medical supplies; treating malnutrition and supporting maternal and child health; conducting vaccination campaigns to prevent disease outbreaks; and offering mental health support to populations impacted by trauma.
The Appeal highlights four key challenges facing the world currently: climate change, conflict, displacement and disease outbreaks. These are responsible for fueling deeper, longer lasting health crises and putting the world’s most vulnerable at greater risk.
The appeal further details the priorities and financial needs for each of the Grade 3 emergencies that WHO is responding to.
With the support of donors and partners, WHO aims to fulfill its unique role in health emergencies, while upholding the principles of international humanitarian law, ensuring that no one is left behind even in the most challenging circumstances.
A call to action
This appeal is about more than just funding – it is a call to action. As crises grow more frequent and severe, the gap between global needs and available resources continues to widen. Supporting WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal is a vital investment in global solidarity and health equity.

a4196.t:
Ahmad Tijjani
The Kano State Government on Monday came out in strong defense of Abdullahi Rogo, the Director General Protocol to Kano State governor over alleged N6.5 billion corruption scandal .
A statement by Mr. Sanusi Bature DawakinTofa, the Director General, Media and Publicity that was made available to Reporters on Monday evening blamed opposition elements of misleading the general public.
The statement titled “KNSG Breaks Silence on Alleged Diversion of N6.5 billion” read in parts :
“The digital media space in the last few days has been awash with a series of false narratives bordering on the accountability, trust, and financial worthiness of some key political aides of the Kano State Government.”
“Central to the case of purported misappropriation, already under litigation at the High Court, is the Director General, Protocol Directorate, Kano State Government House, Alh. Abdullahi Rogo.”
One of the ill-intended narratives, most likely sponsored, was a publication on Daily Nigerian, a Kano-based online news platform, on August 22nd, 2025, which particularly drew government attention to the allegation of withdrawal and diversion of ₦6.5 billion from the state treasury.
Without prejudice to the ongoing litigation on the matter, the state government is obliged to avail the public with the nitty-gritty of the Directorate of Protocol’s operations at Kano Government House, which is not different from structures obtainable in all states and the federal government.
First, government makes bold to say every cash outflow into Ministries, Departments, and Agencies is properly budgeted with clear codes well spelt out in the fiscal policy of the state. Hence, no individual in government MDAs handles public funds without proper designated purpose.
The Directorate of Protocol, Kano State Government, handles critical responsibilities in Government House and key operations in the Office of the Chief Executive of the state. These responsibilities cover but are not limited to logistics, accommodation, welfare, and management of the Governor’s itineraries within and outside the country.
The Directorate of Protocol is equally entrusted to provide required logistics to VIPs and VVIPs, which include the Presidency, Ministers, foreign aides, and other diplomatic visitors on official state visits to the Governor. The large number of personalities captured in this category also includes ordinary citizens that mostly attract the special attention of the Governor.
Expectedly, over 95 per cent of the responsibility of the Directorate of Protocol involves large volumes of financial transactions and more often than not, settles liabilities incurred on the state at the instance of His Excellency.
While the administration of Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf will remain focused on governance and maintain its position on financial prudence, accountability, transparency, and zero tolerance for corruption, the government will not sacrifice the integrity of its aides to deliberate acts of political blackmail being orchestrated by unpatriotic elements of society.
The government is also not in doubt of the credibility of the Director General, Directorate of Protocol, Government House, Hon. Abdullahi Ibrahim Rogo.
More importantly, the New Nigerian Peoples Party (NNPP) administration will remain open to lawful, fair, and unbiased criticism within the ambit of the law, but will not succumb to easy blackmail through misinformation.
“Once again, for clarity, the Office of Protocol in any government or institution is purely administrative in function. Its mandate is to coordinate official engagements, state visits, receptions, ceremonial events, and logistics including handling honorarium, and other interventions as well as special assignments. It is not an independent spending office and does not undertake any financial transactions outside established rules and approvals. Every action undertaken by the Protocol Office is done within the framework of the law and with the express approval of the government the under a designated budget code”
“The allegations being peddled are therefore nothing more than a work of fiction, carefully crafted by political opponents who have resorted to blackmail and propaganda in their desperation to remain relevant ahead of the 2027 elections.”

a4232.t:
The United Nations has expressed grave concerns about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where escalating violence is severely restricting access to vulnerable populations. The fighting, particularly in North and South Kivu provinces, has left aid organizations struggling to reach those in need.
Following intense clashes in Goma last week, a fragile calm has settled over the city, but tensions remain high, according to UN News. While sporadic gunfire has decreased within Goma itself, fighting continues in surrounding areas, especially in Sake, northwest of the city. The UN peacekeeping mission, MONUSCO, is focused on protecting its personnel and the civilians sheltering in its compounds while conducting patrols to assess the situation and facilitate the delivery of essential supplies.
Goma’s airport has been closed since January 26, and key access routes, including the RN2 highway, are blocked. The border between Goma and Gisenyi, Rwanda, has also been shut down since January 28. The UN is urgently calling for the creation of humanitarian corridors to allow the safe passage of displaced people seeking refuge and the delivery of vital aid.
The situation is equally dire in South Kivu, where routes to Minova have been cut off since January 18, effectively isolating communities in need of humanitarian assistance. Negotiations are underway to establish a corridor for emergency aid.
The renewed fighting, involving M23 rebels, has intensified an already protracted crisis that has claimed thousands of lives and displaced countless individuals. In Kinshasa, protests have erupted, with demonstrators targeting embassies to express their frustration with perceived international inaction.
The conflict has also sparked tensions between regional leaders. A recent exchange between the presidents of South Africa and Rwanda highlighted the complexities of the situation. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa cited the deaths of 13 South African soldiers in eastern DRC, attributing the escalation to the “M23 rebel group and the Rwandan Defense Forces (RDF).” His use of the term “militia” to describe the Rwandan forces drew a sharp rebuke from Rwandan President Paul Kagame, who, in a series of posts on X (formerly Twitter), condemned what he called “deliberate distortions” and “lies” in the South African statements, insisting that the RDF is an army, not a militia.
Amidst this volatile environment, the UN has announced the appointment of Brazilian General Ulisses De Mesquita Gomes as the new MONUSCO force commander. He has pledged to work with all mission components to “protect civilians” and contribute to building a better future for the Congolese people.
MONUSCO peacekeepers are actively supporting the Congolese armed forces and regional troops in their fight against the M23 rebels, including providing direct artillery support.

a4350.t:
Pelo menos 19,5 milhões de pessoas vão precisar de ajuda, este ano no Iémen, segundo a Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU), que manifestou preocupação com as crianças subnutridas.
O povo do Iémen continua a enfrentar uma grave crise humanitária e de proteção civil”, disse a subsecretária-geral interina da ONU para os Assuntos Humanitários (OCHA, na sigla em Inglês), Joyce Msuya, ao Conselho de Segurança.
“Pelo menos 19,5 milhões de pessoas no Iémen vão precisar de assistência humanitária e proteção este ano, mais 1,3 milhões do que em 2024”, salientou.
A responsável da ONU acrescentou que “quase metade” da população do país, ou seja, mais de 17 milhões de pessoas, “não consegue satisfazer as suas necessidades alimentares básicas”, manifestando preocupação pelos “mais marginalizados”, como as mulheres e as raparigas ou os 4,8 milhões de deslocados.
Entre os que correm maior risco, “quase metade das crianças com menos de cinco anos sofrem de atraso grave de crescimento devido à subnutrição”, insistiu.
O nível “terrível” do surto de cólera também aumentou a carga sobre um sistema de saúde já “severamente sobrecarregado”.
a4350.en:
Almost 20 million people need humanitarian aid in Yemen

At least 19.5 million people will need aid in Yemen this year, according to the United Nations (UN), which expressed concern about malnourished children.

"The people of Yemen continue to face a grave humanitarian and civil protection crisis," said the UN Acting Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Joyce Msuya, to the Security Council.

"At least 19.5 million people in Yemen will need humanitarian assistance and protection this year, 1.3 million more than in 2024," she stressed.

The UN official added that "almost half" of the country's population, that is, more than 17 million people, "cannot meet their basic food needs," expressing concern for the "most marginalised," such as women and girls and the 4.8 million displaced people.

Among those at greatest risk, "almost half of children under five suffer from severe stunting due to malnutrition," she insisted.

The "terrible" level of the cholera outbreak has also increased the burden on an already "severely overstretched" health system.

a4540.t:
Cette contribution précieuse de l’Ambassade du Royaume de Belgique en faveur des populations touchées par l’insécurité alimentaire dans plusieurs régions du Mali  a fait l’objet d’une cérémonie de remerciement qui a réuni, hier mardi, au siège du Commissariat à la Sécurité Alimentaire, Mohamed Ag Redwane Ali,  le chargé d’affaire de l’Ambassade, son excellence Patrick  Deboeck et le Directeur  pays par intérim du Programme Alimentaire Mondial, Ibrahima Diallo.  
A l’ouverture de cette rencontre, le chargé d’affaires  de l’Ambassade de la Belgique, son excellence Patrick  Deboeck, a  indiqué que l’aide humanitaire apportée par son pays a pour objectifs
 de sauver les vies, d’alléger les souffrances et de préserver la dignité humaine des populations touchées par les crises et catastrophes. Le Mali figure  parmi les  pays du Sahel  bénéficiant  de l’aide humanitaire prolongée du Royaume  de la Belgique,  qui depuis plus d’un an, se positionne  comme chef de file des bailleurs humanitaires aux côtés de l’Allemagne et  de la Suisse. Selon le diplomate, l’’agriculture et la sécurité alimentaire constituent des secteurs clés de la coopération belge au développement.
En répondre à ces besoins croissants et de contribuer à endiguer l’insécurité alimentaire et la malnutrition,  Patrick  Deboeck  souligne que le Programme alimentaire mondial  constitue  un partenaire privilégié  de son pays qui, selon lui, a récemment signé un accord de financement pluriannuel. Au Mali, poursuit le chargé d’affaires,  la Belgique soutient un projet de 3 millions d’euros, soit près de 2 milliards FCFA,  à travers lequel elle contribue à une meilleure sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle.  D’après lui,  cette aide alimentaire d’urgence consiste en premier lieu  à soutenir des populations vulnérables et des Personnes Déplacées Internes  (PDI) durant et après des chocs en leur fournissant des bons alimentaires ou des transferts de fonds inconditionnel. Ce,  afin qu’ils puissent satisfaire leurs besoins alimentaires de base. Et en second lieu, ajoute-t-il, l’aide nutritionnelle vise à assister les enfants de moins de 5 ans souffrant de malnutrition sévère. « Ils recevront à travers ce projet une ration quotidienne afin de fournir trois repas nutritifs par jour », a détaillé le chargé d’affaires, précisant  cela permettra à lutter contre la malnutrition chez les enfants et à contribuer au développement de l'économie locale en proposant aux soignants des menus nutritifs et diversifiés provenant de fournisseurs locaux. Dans ce montant susmentionné, une enveloppe de 500.000 d’euros  est allouée au financement d’UNHAS, une agence dont le travail est indispensable pour assurer l’accès de l’aide aux populations les plus vulnérables, a précisé  le diplomate Belge.
Pour sa part, le Directeur  pays par intérim du PAM, Ibrahima Diallo a décrit un tableau sombre de la  situation alimentaire au Mali  qui, selon ses explications, reste préoccupante dans certaines régions du pays.  Il a cité dans la foulée  le chiffre du  Cadre Harmonisé de mars 2024 qui  fait état environ 1 400 000 de personnes en situation d’insécurité alimentaire aiguë. Les causes s’expliquent, selon lui, par l’aggravation de l’insécurité et les chocs climatiques qui  ont engendré les déplacements de  ces populations. « La détérioration de la situation sécuritaire dans certaines régions du pays a également fortement affecté l’agriculture, la pêche et l’élevage et a considérablement réduit les moyens d’existence de nombreuses communautés », a ajouté le Directeur pays par intérim comme d’autres causes ayant entrainées les déplacements des populations. A cela s’ajoute  la campagne agricole 2023-2024 jugée moyenne à bonne,  avec le prix des denrées alimentaires qui  restent très élevés privant l’accès des ménages les plus pauvres à une alimentation adéquate.
Ce faisant, Ibrahima Diallo  a indiqué que  grâce à la généreuse contribution de 3 millions d’euros du l’Ambassade du Royaume  de Belgique, le PAM pourra apporter une assistance vitale à près de 47 000 personnes,  essentiellement des déplacées internes dans les zones les plus touchées par l'insécurité alimentaire pendant quatre mois. « Cette assistance  permettra de répondre  aux  besoins alimentaires de base  des communautés affectées par les crises susmentionnées pendant et après les chocs »,a  indiqué le représentant du PAM,  annonçant que près de 6 000 accompagnants (principalement des mères) recevront une ration alimentaire trois fois par jour sur une période de 3 mois.  « Ce soutien crucial aux parents d’enfants atteints de malnutrition leur permet de rester avec et auprès de leurs enfants durant le traitement et leur donner une chance de recouvrer rapidement la santé »,  a souhaité Ibrahima Diallo.
Le ministre commissaire à la Sécurité Alimentaire, Mohamed Ag Redwane Ali, a exprimé  la reconnaissance du peuple malien à l’ambassade du Royaume de Belgique  en indiquant  cet appui important permettra  au PAM d’étoffer  son programme d’assistance au Mali.  Selon lui,  ce sont  41 491 personnes qui bénéficieront  de cette aide alimentaire d’urgence pendant une période de 4 mois.  Les personnes bénéficiaires touchées par l’insécurité alimentaire  sont les régions de Kayes, Koulikoro, Sikasso, Ségou, Mopti, Ménaka, Gao, Tombouctou et Kidal.

This valuable contribution from the Embassy of the Kingdom of Belgium in favour of populations affected by food insecurity in several regions of Mali was the subject of a thank-you ceremony that brought together yesterday, Tuesday, at the headquarters of the Food Security Commission, Mohamed Ag Redwane Ali, the Embassy's charge d'affaires, His Excellency Patrick Deboeck, and the interim Country Director of the World Food Programme, Ibrahima Diallo.

At the opening of this meeting, the charge d'affaires of the Embassy of Belgium, His Excellency Patrick Deboeck, indicated that the humanitarian aid provided by his country aims to save lives, alleviate suffering and preserve the human dignity of populations affected by crises and disasters. Mali is among the Sahel countries benefiting from the Kingdom of Belgium's extended humanitarian aid, which for more than a year has positioned itself as the lead humanitarian donor alongside Germany and Switzerland. According to the diplomat, agriculture and food security are key sectors of Belgian development cooperation.

In order to respond to these growing needs and to help stem food insecurity and malnutrition, Patrick Deboeck stressed that the World Food Programme is a privileged partner of his country, which, according to him, recently signed a multi-year funding agreement. In Mali, the charge d'affaires continued, Belgium is supporting a project of 3 million euros, or nearly 2 billion FCFA, through which it contributes to better food and nutritional security. According to him, this emergency food aid consists first of supporting vulnerable populations and Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) during and after shocks by providing them with food vouchers or unconditional cash transfers, so that they can meet their basic food needs. And secondly, he added, the nutritional aid aims to assist children under 5 suffering from severe malnutrition. "Through this project they will receive a daily ration in order to provide three nutritious meals a day," the charge d'affaires detailed, specifying that this will help fight malnutrition among children and contribute to the development of the local economy by offering caregivers nutritious and diversified menus from local suppliers. Within the aforementioned amount, an envelope of 500,000 euros is allocated to the funding of UNHAS, an agency whose work is indispensable to ensuring that aid reaches the most vulnerable populations, the Belgian diplomat specified.

For his part, the interim Country Director of WFP, Ibrahima Diallo, painted a bleak picture of the food situation in Mali which, according to his explanations, remains worrying in certain regions of the country. He then cited the figure from the March 2024 Cadre Harmonise, which reports about 1,400,000 people in acute food insecurity. The causes are explained, according to him, by the worsening of insecurity and by climate shocks that have caused the displacement of these populations. "The deterioration of the security situation in certain regions of the country has also strongly affected agriculture, fishing and livestock farming and has considerably reduced the livelihoods of many communities," added the interim Country Director, among other causes that led to the displacement of populations. To this is added the 2023-2024 agricultural season, judged average to good, with food prices remaining very high, depriving the poorest households of access to adequate food.

Accordingly, Ibrahima Diallo indicated that thanks to the generous contribution of 3 million euros from the Embassy of the Kingdom of Belgium, WFP will be able to provide vital assistance to nearly 47,000 people, essentially internally displaced persons in the areas most affected by food insecurity, for four months. "This assistance will make it possible to meet the basic food needs of the communities affected by the aforementioned crises during and after the shocks," said the WFP representative, announcing that nearly 6,000 caregivers (mainly mothers) will receive a food ration three times a day over a period of 3 months. "This crucial support to the parents of children suffering from malnutrition allows them to stay with and beside their children during treatment and gives them a chance to recover their health quickly," Ibrahima Diallo hoped.

The Minister Commissioner for Food Security, Mohamed Ag Redwane Ali, expressed the gratitude of the Malian people to the Embassy of the Kingdom of Belgium, indicating that this important support will allow WFP to expand its assistance programme in Mali. According to him, 41,491 people will benefit from this emergency food aid over a period of 4 months. The beneficiaries affected by food insecurity are in the regions of Kayes, Koulikoro, Sikasso, Segou, Mopti, Menaka, Gao, Timbuktu and Kidal.

By Seltue Karweaye Sr.
On January 22, 2024, Joseph N. Boakai was inaugurated as the 26th President of Liberia. His swearing-in ceremony took place in the capital city, Monrovia, amidst a crowd of supporters, dignitaries, and members of the international community. President Boakai’s inauguration symbolizes a pivotal moment in Liberia’s political landscape as he takes on the responsibilities of leading the nation.
During his inaugural address, he outlined his vision for the country, emphasizing unity, development, and the importance of addressing pressing issues such as corruption, economic recovery, social justice, etc. As Liberia embarked on this new chapter, the hope was that President Boakai’s leadership would foster positive change and advance the nation’s democratic ideals.
As Boakai stepped into his new role, he confronted the daunting reality of a nation with a shattered economy. The legacy of mismanagement and ineffective governance left by his predecessor, George Weah loomed large, creating significant challenges for Boakai. Corruption had infiltrated the very fabric of government, permeating various levels and fostering a pervasive atmosphere of mistrust. Citizens struggled against the harsh realities of a glaring lack of accountability and transparency among their leaders. Furthermore, the reckless depletion of foreign reserves dealt a severe blow to the nation’s financial stability, exacerbating the crisis and leaving the country vulnerable.
However, as Boakai settled into his role, a series of formidable challenges emerged, each one testing his resolve and capacity to steer the nation toward progress. These challenges were further amplified by the troubled legacy left by the previous administration of George Weah, during which many systemic issues were exacerbated, creating a complex web of obstacles that hampered progress.
Statistical indicators paint a concerning picture of the economic situation in Liberia. By the end of 2024, the inflation rate reached 8.2%, significantly affecting the cost of basic necessities. For example, the national average price for a 25 kg bag of rice has risen to LD 3,900, while the price of gasoline per gallon is LD775 and fuel oil per gallon is LD840.
To compound these issues, the value of the Liberian dollar has fallen by more than 21%, creating a considerable financial burden for citizens. Specifically, the exchange rate deteriorated from 157 LRD to 1 USD in February 2023 and further declined to 189 LRD to 1 USD by January 2025. This sharp depreciation has severely diminished household purchasing power, leaving many families struggling to afford essential needs such as food, healthcare, and education.
Food security in Liberia has demonstrated a concerning and uneven trajectory over recent years. In the latest 2024 Global Hunger Index (GHI), Liberia ranks 120th out of 127 countries for which sufficient data is available to calculate hunger scores. With an alarming GHI score of 31.9, the level of hunger in the country is classified as serious. This dire situation is further illustrated by the findings of the Social Cohesion and Reconciliation Index (SCORE), which indicates a significant decline in food security from 2018 to 2024. The data reveals that a staggering 80% of Liberians face the daunting challenge of providing sufficient food for their families, highlighting the extensive scope of food insecurity in the nation.
The human toll of these economic hardships is deeply distressing and highlights the pervasive nature of poverty across the nation. Recent statistics indicate that nearly 30% of Liberia’s population is living below the extreme international poverty line of $2.15 per person per day. When assessed against the middle-income poverty benchmark of $3.65, this number swells to nearly 70%. The poverty faced by many Liberians is not solely monetary; a significant portion of the population experiences multiple dimensions of deprivation, which includes limited access to essential services such as education, healthcare, and clean water, further complicating their ability to escape the cycle of poverty.
During Boakai’s first year, the administration faced significant challenges, largely due to the absence of a coherent organizing principle and an unifying vision for governance. This lack of clarity and direction has led to a disorganized and chaotic approach to leadership, which has raised concerns among citizens and observers alike.
One glaring indication of Boakai’s lack of preparedness for his role is the evident absence of comprehensive analysis and strategic planning in the policies he has enacted since assuming office. In the realm of political economics, such decisions are often categorized as “stroke-of-the-pen” actions—choices that can be made swiftly and with little difficulty. While this approach may be practical in certain situations, many decisions carry profound and lasting ramifications that demand a more thoughtful and deliberate consideration, rather than impulsive execution.
Following President Boakai’s swearing-in ceremony, there were evident delays in the appointment of key officials. The process of nominating individuals to various positions unfolded over three months after the inauguration, with some nominations occurring sporadically, spaced approximately a week apart. Compounding the issue, several appointments were not publicly announced, which contributed to a general lack of transparency regarding the appointment process. This opacity further undermined the public’s right to be informed about significant governance decisions.
According to the Center for Transparency and Accountability (CENTAL), a prominent civil society organization in Liberia and the national chapter of Transparency International, of the total 1,306 appointments made, 38 were embroiled in controversy. This included 13 appointments that were altered or modified after their initial announcement and another 25 appointments that became ineffective.
The latter group included cases where appointments were revoked by the President, instances of resignation, legal proceedings, or situations where current officeholders refused to continue in their roles.
The significant volume of withdrawals and the circumstances surrounding these changes raise critical questions. Firstly, they call into doubt the thoroughness and effectiveness of the vetting procedures that were or were not implemented during this process. Secondly, there is concern regarding the broader awareness of the specific restrictions that apply to certain positions, which may have influenced these decisions. Finally, the motivations behind such numerous alterations to the appointments remain unclear, further contributing to the public’s uncertainty and mistrust in the administration’s handling of appointments.
Despite a complicated and often controversial history in public service, President Joseph Boakai has appointed several individuals to key positions within public service. These appointments reflect both trust and concern given the backgrounds of those selected. One significant appointment was S. Tornorlah Varpilah. appointed as the Chairman of the Liberia Maritime Authority (LMA). Varpilah’s responsibilities include overseeing maritime operations and ensuring compliance with international maritime laws. He was designated by the National Legislature to restitute public funds.
Also, Abdullah Kamara, recently appointed by President Boakai as the Acting Chairperson of the Liberia Telecommunications Authority (LTA), is facing serious allegations of corruption. A comprehensive audit conducted by the General Auditing Commission (GAC) revealed that during his time as CEO of TAMMA Corporation, Kamara was involved in making unauthorized payments totaling L$262,844,500 and US$450,000. These financial transactions reportedly took place without adhering to established procurement protocols, indicating a significant breach of trust and accountability.
Furthermore, Kamara is accused of orchestrating a $2.6 million scam that has purportedly deprived over 10,000 young Liberians of vital digital literacy opportunities. This project was designed to accelerate digital literacy and improve internet connectivity among the nation’s youth, but it allegedly failed to deliver any tangible results. Reports suggest that the funding for this initiative simply vanished, leaving many young individuals without access to the promised training and resources.
Despite the gravity of these allegations and the implications they carry for public trust in the administration, Abdullah Kamara continues to serve as the Acting Chairperson of the Liberia Telecommunication Authority (LTA). His ongoing position raises significant questions about President Boakai’s commitment to addressing corruption and enforcing accountability within his administration. In light of these findings, the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL) has publicly called for Kamara’s dismissal, urging that the GAC’s audit findings warrant immediate action to restore credibility and integrity to the government.
Another significant appointment is that of Daniel Johnson, who has taken on the role of Secretary General for the Roberts Flight Information Region. It is crucial to note that Johnson is currently sought by the United States government for allegedly defrauding the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) out of approximately $1.9 million. This situation raises serious concerns about the integrity of his appointment.
Nortu Jappah has been named the head of the National Insurance Company of Liberia, where he will be responsible for managing the nation’s insurance affairs. However, Jappah has a controversial background; he was reportedly “forced to resign” from his previous position as Managing Director of the Liberia Water and Sewer Corporation (LWSC) in 2012. This resignation was linked to his involvement in a corruption scandal concerning the importation of substandard pipes and chemicals, which had severe implications for public health and infrastructure.
Further complicating the situation, Patrick Sandike was appointed as the Deputy Managing Director for Technical Services at LWSC. Sandike has a troubled history, having been dismissed from the institution for corruption during his tenure as Operations Engineer. His dismissal raises concerns about the effectiveness of oversight in the appointment process.
Rudolph Merab has been appointed as the Managing Director of the Forestry Development Authority (FDA). Merab has a notorious reputation linked to illegal logging activities during Liberia’s civil war, casting doubt on his suitability for a position that is supposed to promote sustainable forestry practices and protect the nation’s natural resources.
Finally, Mohammed Maladho Bah has been appointed as the Special Presidential Envoy for Investment. However, his reputation is marred by allegations that he defrauded Liberians while posing as a dealer of used cars, further complicating the perception of his role within the government. These appointments reflect a broader context of challenges facing the Boakai administration as it grapples with issues of accountability, corruption, and the public’s trust in government institutions.
In a series of controversial appointments, the President has been accused of engaging in nepotism by favoring relatives of public officials and his political allies. A notable example is the selection of Sirleaf Tyler, the brother of Senator Alex J. Tyler, who was appointed as Minister of Transport. In this vital role, he is tasked with shaping and directing the nation’s transportation policies and overseeing the development of essential infrastructure.
Similarly, Nancy Moye, the wife of Senator Prince Moye, has secured a position on the board of the Liberia Petroleum Refinery Company (LPRC). This company is crucial for managing the country’s petroleum resources, making her appointment both significant and influential in the energy sector. The late Senator Prince Y. Johnson’s daughter, Daybah E. Johnson was appointed as Assistant Minister for Regional Labor Affairs.
Further illustrating this trend is S. Tornolar Varpilah, the husband of Senator Darbah Varpilah, who has taken on the role of Chairman of the Board of the Liberia Maritime Authority (LMA). This position is essential for the regulation of maritime activities, ensuring the safety of operations at sea, and guiding the country’s maritime policies.
Moreover, the next generation of the Varpilah family also makes its mark in public service, with Senator Varpilah’s children—Nee-Alah T. Varpilah and Feetor Varpilah—assuming significant roles as the Director-General of the Liberia Institute of Public Administration (LIPA) and the Deputy Director-General of the National Insurance Company of Liberia (NICOL), respectively. These appointments paint a striking picture of a political landscape where familial ties and political connections appear to overshadow meritocratic principles, raising important questions about the administration’s dedication to governance rooted in competence and capability rather than personal relationships.
President Boakai has made a conscious effort by intentionally avoiding the appointment of immediate family members to significant government roles, a decision that reflects a commitment to maintaining integrity within his administration. Despite this commendable effort, he has attracted criticism for choosing to appoint Jacob T. Kabakole, a well-connected and influential nephew, as the Chairman of the Board of the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA). This decision has raised concerns about nepotism and the potential impact on the governance of the crucial petroleum sector in Liberia.
In truth, the first year of President Joseph Boakai was characterized by a notable level of weakness and ineffectiveness, struggling to address the myriad of urgent challenges that Liberia faces today. During its first year, the administration has seen a considerable spike in governance costs, raising concerns about financial prudence and sustainability. For the upcoming fiscal year 2025, President Boakai has put forth a budget proposal amounting to $851.8 million. A considerable part of this budget, specifically $745.69 million, is earmarked for recurrent expenditures, which represents a staggering 87.5% of the total budget. This proposal signifies the first comprehensive annual financial plan presented by the Boakai administration and reflects its fiscal priorities.
Over the past 12 months, the Boakai administration has markedly ramped up its borrowing activities, accumulating over $236 million in debt within just one year. This surge in borrowing is particularly concerning given prior assurances from the administration that it would take steps to rein in excessive borrowing practices. Such a reckless financial strategy has contributed to a concerning rise in the national debt, which exceeded $2.5 billion by the conclusion of September 2024, based on the latest figures provided by the Debt Management Office in its third-quarter fiscal report. This alarming trajectory raises critical questions regarding the government’s fiscal responsibility and its long-term economic strategies, especially in light of the pressing challenges facing the nation.
During his campaign, then-candidate, Joseph Boakai made a significant commitment to the citizens, pledging that upon assuming office, he would ensure that no vehicle would become stuck in the mud within his first 100 days. His administration aimed to improve infrastructure nationwide, with a particular focus on making all major corridors accessible and safe for travel. However, a year after taking office, the reality has proven to be different. Numerous reports have surfaced from various regions, highlighting the deteriorating conditions of the roads. Many major routes are now in such disrepair that they have become virtually impassable during the rainy season, leading to widespread dissatisfaction among the public. Citizens have expressed their frustration, demanding action to address the urgent need for road maintenance and improvement.
The security situation under the administration of Boakai is extremely concerning and has reached a critical point. Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, experiences a high crime rate, prompting the U.S. Department of State’s Diplomatic Security Service (DSS) to classify the city as a location with a CRITICAL threat level. This designation indicates the potential for a crime that could directly impact U.S. government officials and their interests, reflecting a serious environment of danger.
In December 2024, a catastrophic fire erupted in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, engulfing the parliament building and significantly destroying essential offices and historical archives. This tragic incident marked the second fire in just one week and occurred shortly after a violent clash between protesters and police. The protesters were advocating for strict adherence to the rule of law during the contentious process of removing the Speaker of the House of Representatives, amidst an ongoing legislative standoff that had sowed division among lawmakers.
In addition to the chaos surrounding the political landscape, reports have emerged detailing a troubling surge in violent crime across the city. Residents have expressed growing concerns about armed robberies, assaults, and other serious offenses perpetrated by organized crime syndicates that seem to operate with relative ease and few consequences.
The local law enforcement agencies are frequently overwhelmed by the sheer volume of criminal activity and often lack the necessary resources, training, and support to manage and mitigate these threats to public safety effectively.
Furthermore, the healthcare system in Liberia is in a state of severe disrepair and neglect. Hospitals are described as being in abysmal conditions, with many wards resembling slaughterhouses due to inadequate sanitation and a lack of basic medical supplies. Primary healthcare clinics have been abandoned, leaving many communities without access to essential health services. The challenges are compounded by crippling electricity tariffs that healthcare facilities cannot afford, which hampers their ability to operate effectively. As a result, many healthcare professionals are leaving the country in search of better opportunities, contributing to a growing healthcare crisis. This neglect reflects a broader trend of governmental indifference towards the needs of the population, particularly the poor, who are left to navigate an increasingly dangerous and unhealthy environment.
Boakai’s administration has encountered a series of significant challenges, primarily stemming from numerous allegations of corruption and a widespread culture of impunity that appears to have permeated the ranks of government officials. Reports have surfaced indicating that before his inauguration, President Boakai requested funding from the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP) to finance the purchase of five high-end Land Cruiser SUVs, each valued at approximately $117,000. This action took place without any constitutional authority and has raised serious concerns about the misallocation of public funds, placing the President under intense public scrutiny and criticism.
In addition to this issue, allegations have emerged suggesting that President Boakai engaged in bribery schemes aimed at influencing key legislative decisions and gaining favor among legislators. This includes claims that he provided financial inducements to lawmakers in a bid to shape the leadership structure within the Legislature, raising further questions about ethical governance and accountability.
Moreover, there are troubling reports regarding Jake Kabakole, the President’s nephew and Officer-in-Charge of the National Oil Company of Liberia (NOCAL). It has been alleged that he authorized the disbursement of $600,000 to contractors under dubious conditions, prompting concerns about the transparency of financial transactions within the government.
Public Works Minister Roland Giddings has publicly acknowledged breaching procurement protocols by awarding road maintenance contracts valued at $22.4 million without adhering to a competitive bidding process. This lack of compliance with established procurement laws not only undermines public trust but also raises red flags regarding the fair allocation of state resources.
Furthermore, reports indicate that a total of 285 pieces of earth-moving equipment were reportedly provided to the Boakai government as part of an agreement with the Guma Group related to the exploration of the Wologizi mountain. However, despite the claims surrounding this partnership, the government has denied that any formal agreement was finalized, adding another layer of complexity to the ongoing scrutiny of its dealings.
In light of these issues, Giddings and several other high-ranking officials have reportedly sought mercy and forgiveness for their actions, indicating a troubling pattern of governance characterized by ethical lapses and a lack of accountability. This collective behavior highlights broader systemic issues within the administration, indicating an urgent need for reform to restore public confidence in the government’s commitment to transparency and ethical conduct.
Compounding these issues, the President failed to release any investigative findings related to the poor planning that characterized the inauguration ceremony, as well as ongoing allegations of mismanagement connected to a program budget of $600,000. Instead, President Boakai publicly expressed unwavering confidence in Madam Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Chairperson of the inaugural committee, which many saw as an attempt to deflect criticism rather than address the underlying problems.
Furthermore, President Boakai is accused of violating the Code of Conduct regarding the declaration of his assets. Instead of declaring his assets before assuming office, he did so 16 days after taking office, raising suspicions about transparency and accountability. To date, appointed government officials have not complied with asset declaration requirements, facing no consequences for their inaction. This lack of accountability persists despite President Boakai’s directive dated November 28, 2024, which instructed all appointed officials to follow the Declaration of Assets requirements specified in the 2014 Code of Conduct.
Recently, the University of Liberia (UL) investigative committee conducted a thorough investigation into allegations of academic fraud involving Commerce Inspector D. Dorr Cooper. The committee concluded that Cooper had illegally obtained an undergraduate degree in Public Administration, a serious violation of academic integrity. According to the findings detailed in their report, Cooper allegedly paid $10,000 to members of the university staff to facilitate his impersonation of a deceased student. This fraudulent act allowed him to graduate under false pretenses.
The investigation was initiated after growing concerns were raised regarding Cooper’s eligibility to graduate shortly before the Alexander Romeo Horton College of Business and Public Administration held its commencement ceremony on September 10, 2024. Despite the clear recommendations outlined in the investigative committee’s report, which included prosecution for Cooper’s unethical actions, President Boakai made the controversial decision to retain D. Dorr Cooper in his position at the Ministry of Commerce, disregarding the committee’s findings and the implications of allowing such misconduct to go unpunished.
President Joseph Boakai stands accused of failing to adhere to constitutional mandates, raising serious concerns about his respect for the rule of law in Liberia. Notably, just three months into his presidency, on April 24, 2024, the Supreme Court issued a significant ruling. The court stated that Boakai’s appointments of individuals to tenured positions in various government institutions directly violated established laws. This ruling not only underscored the importance of following legal protocols but also highlighted the potential dangers of neglecting them.
Despite the Supreme Court’s explicit warnings, President Boakai proceeded to appoint Cllr. Murphy Kanneh as the officer-in-charge of the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP). This controversial decision ignited a firestorm of debate, particularly surrounding the validity and legitimacy of leadership within the organization. In the face of this upheaval, Madam Carmerna Cephas Yeke, who had been serving as the deputy director-general of NASSCORP, exhibited remarkable resolve and bravery. She stood her ground against Cllr. Kanneh, who sought to assert complete managerial control over NASSCORP. The ensuing standoff between the new officer-in-charge and the deputy director-general was tense and filled with palpable drama, capturing the public’s attention. The atmosphere grew increasingly tense when, just two weeks later, President Boakai unexpectedly dismissed Madam Yeke from her position. Citing “gross insubordination to the Office of the President,” the president’s reasoning sparked a wave of concerns regarding the administration’s dedication to due process and its respect for established institutional roles.
The suspension of J. Aloysius Tarlue, who serves as the Executive Governor of the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL), has sparked considerable concern and intrigue. Many are questioning the nature of his suspension, particularly since it was implemented without any accompanying compensation. This unexpected decision was prompted by a comprehensive report from the General Auditing Commission (GAC), which uncovered serious compliance failures at the CBL spanning from 2018 to 2023. In stark contrast to Tarlue’s predicament, Madam Nyemadi D. Pearson, the Deputy Governor for Operations at the CBL, was permitted to resign and received a public expression of gratitude from Boakai for her contributions. This divergence in responses has fueled speculation among observers that Pearson may have walked away with a substantial compensation package, raising further questions about the consistency and fairness in how the bank handles its leadership transitions amidst ongoing difficulties.
Also, the recent indefinite suspension of Madam Davidetta Brown-Lansanah, the Chairperson of the National Elections Commission (NEC), by President Joseph Boakai, raises serious concerns about the integrity of our democratic processes. This action is emblematic of a government prepared to bypass constitutional norms to silence opposition voices and consolidate power within its ranks. Madam Brown-Lansanah has played a crucial role in overseeing the electoral landscape, ensuring fair and transparent elections that reflect the will of the people. By suspending her, the administration is not only undermining the independence of the NEC but also sending a worrying message about its commitment to democratic principles.
The timing of this suspension is especially troubling, as the country is set to conduct by-elections in just two months for Nimba County. This election is particularly significant following the death of influential Senator Prince Yomie Johnson, a former warlord, whose passing has left a notable void in the political landscape. With such a critical election on the horizon, the suspension of the NEC Chairperson raises questions about the integrity of the upcoming electoral process and whether the government is attempting to exert undue influence over the Commission. This situation calls for vigilant scrutiny from the public and civil society, as the future of our democracy hangs in the balance.
Upon taking office, Boakai inherited a Liberia that was already fragmented along various lines, yet he exacerbated these divisions during his first year in office. The societal rifts that separate us have intensified significantly, creating an increasingly polarized environment. A particularly concerning aspect of his administration has been his pattern of appointments, which overwhelmingly favor individuals from the North-Central region of Liberia. Specifically, more than half (57 percent) of those appointed to lead key ministries, departments, and agencies (MDAs) hail from this region, which includes Lofa, Bong, and Nimba counties. This region’s dominance in his appointments suggests a deliberate strategy to strengthen his base of support among those who backed his presidential bid. In contrast, individuals who are suspected of aligning with opposition parties have been systematically overlooked for positions of responsibility. This practice not only undermines the principles of inclusivity and fairness but also raises concerns about governance and representation in a country that is in dire need of unity.
In May 2024, President Boakai took a historic step toward addressing the deep-rooted injustices of Liberia’s past by signing an executive order that established a war crimes court in the nation. This landmark decision represented the culmination of decades of tireless efforts by advocates and victims alike to seek justice for those affected by Liberia’s two devastating civil wars, which raged from 1989 to 2003. These brutal conflicts claimed the lives of approximately 250,000 individuals, leaving a profound scar on the country’s collective memory. The newly formed court is intended to provide a vital avenue for accountability, ensuring that the serious human rights violations that marred this chaotic period do not go unpunished and that the voices of the victims are finally heard.
By November 2024, as part of his administration’s strategic initiative to enhance Liberia’s diplomatic footprint on the global stage, President Boakai appointed Lewis Brown as Ambassador-Designate to represent Liberia at the Permanent Mission to the United Nations in New York City. Brown’s nomination ignited vigorous debates about the implications of appointing individuals with ties to previous conflicts to critical positions in international diplomacy. This discussion reflected broader concerns about the complexities of reconciliation and the potential impact of such appointments on Liberia’s image and diplomatic relations as it seeks to forge a new path forward.
Also, President Joseph Boakai has recently come under fire for his frequent use of chartered flights to attend official functions outside the country. This has drawn attention given the Unity Party’s previous criticisms of former President George Weah for similarly using private jets while in office. The contradictions between past statements and current actions have raised eyebrows among political observers and constituents alike. To clarify the situation, Fofana, the Presidential Press Secretary, addressed the media. He emphasized that there are circumstances where flying on chartered flights becomes necessary for the president. He stated, “Sometimes, taking chartered flights is not just a preference but a necessity. When the president is traveling to attend a significant meeting that requires his presence and is located within a relatively short distance, it is crucial that he can arrive efficiently and effectively.”
Fofana’s recent statements shed light on the political landscape in Liberia, particularly in relation to Senator Darius Dillon from Montserrado County. Dillon, a notable supporter of the “Rescue” government, has made headlines with his public apology regarding past criticisms. He acknowledged the hypocrisy in leveraging allegations about private jet usage as a political weapon against President George Weah in 2023. This admission suggests a significant change in the dialogue surrounding the use of chartered flights by government officials and raises questions about the principles of fairness and political accountability.
This developing conversation underscores the current complexities of political accountability in Liberia, especially in light of the criticisms previously directed at President Weah by his opponents. President Joseph Boakai and his Unity Party have often condemned Weah’s use of a private jet, portraying it as an extravagant expense borne by the Liberian taxpayer. The irony of this situation is now becoming more apparent, as Boakai’s camp has also faced scrutiny for similar behaviors. In an attempt to clarify his position, President Weah openly confirmed his access to a private jet. He insists that the aircraft, valued at millions of dollars, was a gift from a friend in Burkina Faso. However, this claim raises important legal and ethical questions, as the acceptance of such a lavish gift is in direct violation of the National Code of Conduct law in Liberia. This legislation explicitly discourages public officials from receiving gifts that could influence their duties or undermine public trust. As this debate unfolds, it highlights the ongoing challenges of maintaining integrity and transparency in leadership within the country.
Evaluating a six-year government based solely on its first year can present a skewed perspective. Nonetheless, the initial year is a critical period for introducing innovative initiatives and laying a solid foundation that is necessary for strengthening the rule of law, enhancing transparency, promoting accountability, and improving overall government performance. President Boakai’s inaugural year has offered a significant glimpse into his intentions and his commitment to addressing the pressing issues of corruption, institutional underperformance, and a wide range of governance challenges that have long plagued the public sector in Liberia.
Unfortunately, the first year of President Boakai’s leadership has primarily been characterized by a “Business As Usual” mentality. This approach indicates a concerning continuity of historical practices that have hindered progress, rather than embracing the transformative change that many citizens hoped to see. Although there have been some noteworthy positive developments, several significant issues remain unresolved and require immediate attention.
For President Boakai and his team to effectively address the multifaceted needs and aspirations of the Liberian people as they embark on the second years of a six years pivotal journey, it is absolutely essential that they fully commit to the core principles of the rule of law, transparency, and inclusive governance. This historical juncture in Liberia’s development does not merely require leadership but demands a comprehensive and strategic approach that recognizes the importance of diverse skill sets and perspectives in crafting effective policies.
Firstly, a commitment to the rule of law is fundamental. This means ensuring that laws are applied consistently and fairly, without favoritism or bias, and that all citizens, regardless of their socio-economic status, have equal access to justice. It is vital that the administration actively works to strengthen judicial systems, promote accountability, and eliminate corruption. By reinforcing these principles, the leadership can cultivate an environment of trust and integrity that resonates with the populace.
In addition to legal adherence, transparency is crucial in building confidence in the government. This involves open communication with the public regarding decision-making processes, budget allocations, and policy implementations. By making information readily accessible and involving citizens in consultations, the administration can create a culture of openness and encourage civic engagement. Town hall meetings, public forums, and online platforms for feedback can serve as effective tools for promoting dialogue between the government and the citizenry.
Equally important is the principle of inclusion, which necessitates actively seeking out and valuing a wide array of expertise and experiences from various sectors of society, including marginalized groups, women, and youth. Rather than relying predominantly on political allies, sycophants, and opportunists looking to further their own interests, the nation needs leaders capable of building diverse teams that reflect the full spectrum of Liberia’s talent. This not only enhances the decision-making process but also empowers citizens and fosters a sense of shared ownership in national progress.
The Liberian people have faced significant hardships and challenges for far too long. We must break away from the patterns of “Business as Usual,” which have perpetuated these struggles and hindered progress. Now is the time to take decisive action and steer Liberia toward a brighter, more prosperous future. By prioritizing reform, accountability, and sustainable development, we can create a society that fosters hope and opportunity for all Liberians. I rest my pen.
About the Author: Seltue R. Karweaye can be reached at karweayee@gmail.com

Namibia recently sent a 350-ton consignment of locally-produced charcoal to the United States.
The export deal, between Africa Burns Charcoal, King Charcoal, and their US trading partner The Good Charcoal Company, is supported by the US government through the US Agency for International Development (USAID).
The hybrid launch event held in Windhoek a week ago, at which many participants joined virtually from the United States, marks the first-ever export of charcoal from Namibia directly to the US market.
US ambassador to Namibia Lisa Johnson and deputy minister of industrialisation Verna Sinimbo were amongst those who witnessed the event.
It also signals the commencement of a trade opportunity that could see Namibia export several thousand tons of premium-grade charcoal to the United States tariff-free each month.
Ambassador Johnson praised the new trade link with the United States, adding “The ‘Forest Stewardship Council’ has coined Namibian charcoal as ‘the greenest charcoal on the planet’, and the charcoal being sent to the United States is FSC-certified in terms of international standards for environmental, economic and social sustainability.”
The Good Charcoal Company is enthusiastic to introduce this particular brand of sustainable charcoal to the US market. Namibian charcoal producers have worked for years to export to the US market, the biggest charcoal consumer in the world.
This first sample for export marks a milestone for the Namibian Charcoal Association (NCA) and its membership. NCA General Manager Michael Degé, speaking on behalf of the exporters Africa Burns Charcoal and King Charcoal, said “the support of development partners, including USAID, has been key in advancing charcoal as a priority sector for export, and the event today represents many months of efforts to meet the necessary entry requirements because we appreciate that the US market is key to this export growth.”
This first export consignment of 350 tons of charcoal to the United States is valued at US$150 000 (over N$2 million).
If the US market is receptive to Namibian charcoal, the Good Charcoal Company intends to import a total of 165 000 tons of Namibian charcoal by September 2022, valued at over US$65 million (approximately N$950 million).
The trade deal is expected to have far-reaching impacts on the charcoal business in Namibia, including job-creation. The deal will have a positive socio-economic impact on communities where it is needed the most, especially as Covid-19 continues to negatively impact Namibia’s economy.

Un nouveau guichet unique du Groupe de la
Banque mondiale en termes de garanties sera disponible dès le 1er juillet
prochain. Il sera mis en place dans le cadre d’une refonte du système de
garantie visant à améliorer la procédure et à offrir des produits innovants.
Le Groupe de la Banque mondiale compte tripler
son montant annuel d’émissions de garanties, pour le porter à 20 milliards de
dollars d’ici 2030. Pour ce faire, une refonte majeure de ses activités dans le
domaine des garanties est annoncée pour permettre de gagner en simplicité, en
accès et en rapidité d’exécution dans le cadre d’une nouvelle plateforme
centralisée et adaptée.
La refonte s’articule autour de six
remaniements relatifs : une structure concentrée de tous les experts en
garantie, une offre de produits simplifiée et complète, un processus
rationalisé pour les examens relatifs aux instruments de garantie, une plus grande
accessibilité aux garanties, une montée en échelle et de nouveaux outils
innovants, précise un communiqué de presse en date à Washington du 28 février
2024. Ces réaménagements annoncés permettront de supprimer les procédures
redondantes, afin d’apporter aux clients transparence et certitude tout au long
du processus et d’améliorer ainsi leur expérience, tout en offrant des produits
de garantie nouveaux et innovants qui permettront au secteur privé de s’engager
davantage dans la résolution des défis actuels du développement.
« Les ressources et l’ingéniosité du secteur
privé nous sont indispensables pour relever les grands défis mondiaux », assure
Ajay Banga, président de la Banque mondiale, cité dans le communiqué. « En
consolidant nos offres, en simplifiant les processus et en améliorant
l'accessibilité, nous assurons aux entreprises un accès plus rapide et plus
facile aux garanties», estime-t-il.
La nouvelle plateforme de garanties de la
Banque mondiale permettra de « fournir des garanties à une plus grande échelle
et plus rapidement, et donc davantage de financements pour contribuer à
résoudre les problèmes les plus urgents dans le monde », renchérit Mark Carney,
envoyé spécial des Nations Unies pour le financement de l’l'action climatique
et coprésident de Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (Gfanz).
Réformes
Le Groupe de la Banque mondiale offre
actuellement à ses clients 20 solutions de garantie disséminées dans l’ensemble
de l’institution, avec des règles, des normes et des processus différents.
Cette multiplicité limite leur potentiel et leur accessibilité. Il est question
de regrouper toutes les garanties du Groupe au sein d’une offre centralisée,
afin de permettre aux clients d’identifier et de sélectionner facilement
l’instrument de garantie le mieux adapté à leurs besoins individuels.
Le groupe d’experts indépendants du G20, dans
son récent rapport sur le renforcement des banques multilatérales de
développement, a appelé à une augmentation du recours aux garanties pour
atténuer les risques et catalyser les financements privés. Ces garanties
constituent l’un des moyens les plus efficaces pour mobiliser des fonds privés
en faveur du climat et du développement. Elles contribueront à inciter les
investisseurs à s'engager davantage dans les économies en développement et à
accélérer les changements positifs.
En facilitant l’accès à l’ensemble des
garanties du Groupe de la Banque mondiale, la nouvelle plateforme de garanties
permettra aux prêteurs et aux emprunteurs de mieux cerner les options
disponibles afin de planifier les investissements avec davantage de certitude,
espère Shriti Vadera, présidente de compagnie d'assurances britannique
«Prudential Plc ».
La nouvelle plateforme reçoit le soutien du
Laboratoire de l’investissement du secteur privé mis sur pied par la Banque
mondiale. « Elle encouragera des réformes telles que l'harmonisation des
structures contractuelles et clarifiera les rôles que les organisations des
secteurs public et privé doivent jouer pour assurer la viabilité des projets »,
selon Noel Quinn, directeur général de Hsbc Holdings Plc, membre dudit
laboratoire.

A new single window of the World Bank Group for guarantees will be available as of 1 July. It will be set up as part of an overhaul of the guarantee system aimed at improving the procedure and offering innovative products.
The World Bank Group intends to triple its annual volume of guarantee issuance, bringing it to 20 billion dollars by 2030. To do so, a major overhaul of its guarantee activities has been announced, to make for greater simplicity, access and speed of execution within a new centralised and adapted platform.
The overhaul is built around six changes relating to: a concentrated structure bringing together all guarantee experts, a simplified and comprehensive product offering, a streamlined process for reviews relating to guarantee instruments, greater accessibility of guarantees, a scaling-up, and new innovative tools, states a press release dated Washington, 28 February 2024. These announced rearrangements will make it possible to eliminate redundant procedures, in order to provide clients with transparency and certainty throughout the process and thereby improve their experience, while offering new and innovative guarantee products that will allow the private sector to engage further in resolving today's development challenges.
"The resources and ingenuity of the private sector are indispensable to us in meeting the great global challenges," asserts Ajay Banga, President of the World Bank, quoted in the press release. "By consolidating our offerings, simplifying processes and improving accessibility, we are giving businesses faster and easier access to guarantees," he considers.
The World Bank's new guarantee platform will make it possible to "provide guarantees on a larger scale and more quickly, and therefore more financing to help solve the world's most urgent problems," adds Mark Carney, United Nations Special Envoy for Climate Action Finance and co-chair of the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (GFANZ).
Reforms
The World Bank Group currently offers its clients 20 guarantee solutions scattered across the institution, with different rules, standards and processes. This multiplicity limits their potential and their accessibility. The aim is to bring together all of the Group's guarantees within a centralised offering, so as to allow clients easily to identify and select the guarantee instrument best suited to their individual needs.
The G20's independent expert group, in its recent report on strengthening multilateral development banks, called for increased use of guarantees to mitigate risk and catalyse private financing. These guarantees are one of the most effective means of mobilising private funds for climate and development. They will help encourage investors to engage further in developing economies and to accelerate positive change.
By facilitating access to the full set of World Bank Group guarantees, the new guarantee platform will allow lenders and borrowers to better grasp the available options in order to plan investments with greater certainty, hopes Shriti Vadera, chair of the British insurance company "Prudential Plc".
The new platform has the support of the Private Sector Investment Lab set up by the World Bank. "It will encourage reforms such as the harmonisation of contractual structures and will clarify the roles that public and private sector organisations must play to ensure the viability of projects," according to Noel Quinn, Chief Executive Officer of HSBC Holdings Plc, a member of that lab.

- Deepening China-Zambia all-weather friendship
LAST week, representatives from China, 53 African countries and the African Union Commission gathered in Changsha and attended the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) ministerial coordinator’s meeting, where the China-Africa Changsha Declaration on Upholding Solidarity and Cooperation of the Global South was issued.
From this meeting, I am pleased to see that the rise and growth of the Global South represents the unstoppable trend of our times and the future of development.
In the face of frequent occurrence of unilateralism, protectionism and economic bullying by a certain country for selfish gains, which has created severe difficulties for the world, China and African countries sent out a strong message for solidarity and cooperation of the Global South.
The message was sent through the Changsha Declaration, in the firm belief that countries should uphold true multilateralism, safeguard the United Nations-centred international system, defend
the World Trade Organisation-centred multilateral trading system and make economic globalisation more open, inclusive, mutually beneficial and balanced, so as to foster a better trade, investment and financing environment for the Global South.
In particular, the international community should give prioritised attention to the economic difficulties and development challenges faced by African countries.
Development assistance to African countries should be increased, not unilaterally slashed, to provide continued support to help African countries improve people’s livelihood, reduce poverty and boost economic and social development.
During the meeting, China announced that it will expand the zero-tariff treatment for 100 percent tariff lines to all 53 African countries having diplomatic relations with it, to help quality products from Africa access the Chinese market.
For the least developed countries in Africa, on top of the zero-tariff treatment for 100 percent tariff lines, China will roll out further measures on market access, inspection and quarantine, and customs clearance to boost trade in goods, enhance skills and technical training, and expand promotion of quality products.
Through implementation of the 10 Partnership Actions of FOCAC, China and Africa will strengthen cooperation in key sectors such as green industries, e-commerce and digital payment, science and technology, and artificial intelligence, while expanding collaboration in security, finance and rule of law.
I believe these measures will substantially advance China-Africa economic and trade relations, accelerate the development of African countries and deliver tangible benefits to both Chinese and African peoples.
China and Zambia are all-weather friends and comprehensive strategic and cooperative partners.
Over the 60 years since the establishment of our diplomatic relations, the two countries have always upheld the principle of mutual respect, equality and common development.
In 2024, trade between China and Zambia reached US$6.703 billion, a 26.5 percent year-on-year growth.
Currently, over 600 Chinese companies are operating in Zambia, with an accumulative investment exceeding US$3.8 billion, creating more than 30,000 local jobs.
In recent years, substantial progress has been made in joint projects, such as the Lusaka-Ndola dual carriageway, the expansion of Mfuwe International Airport, Kitumba Mine, Luanshya 28 Shaft, the 100MW Chisamba Solar Plant and Lubambe Mine deep shaft.
These are tangible projects that are boosting Zambia’s economic and social development and delivering real benefits to both countries and our peoples.
This year marks the 25th anniversary of FOCAC and the inaugural year for implementing the outcomes of the 2024 FOCAC Beijing Summit.
Under the FOCAC framework, China has assisted Zambia in projects such as sports facilities, hospitals, schools, agricultural technology demonstration centre, malaria control centre, small hydropower stations and photovoltaic power plants.
In early May this year, 108,300 doses of oral cholera vaccines donated by China arrived in Lusaka.
To address Zambia’s needs, China will further assist in constructing milling plants and water supply projects, while collaborating with Zambia to establish a cholera vaccine manufacturing plant through a joint venture and provide medical supplies for HIV/AIDS response.
The Tanzania-Zambia Railway (TAZARA) is a household name in both countries, hailed as a monument of China-Africa friendship.
Currently, the negotiation for TAZARA revitalisation is making good progress and the project is expected to be launched within this year.
With the successful revitalisation of railway, Zambia will play a more important role as a land-linked country, with its advantage as a regional transportation hub further enhanced.
The TAZARA economic corridor will emerge and industrial parks, economic zones and new urban centres will spring up along the route.
Industries such as transportation and logistics, mining, agriculture, green energy and equipment manufacturing will flourish, creating a significant number of job opportunities and helping Zambia climb up the value chain and achieve prosperity for its people.
Inclusive cooperation represents the right way forward for the world, and mutual benefit meets the aspirations of the people.
No matter how the international situation evolves, China’s door to Zambia and Africa will only open wider.
I am confident that by advancing modernisation hand in hand, China and Zambia will further deepen the all-weather friendship and practical cooperation, jointly contributing to solidarity and cooperation of the Global South and a brighter future for our world.
The author is Chinese Ambassador to Zambia
